previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted with abdominal pain exacerbated by heavy alcohol use. Imaging ruled out gallbladder disease but confirmed cirrhosis and portal hypertension. His pain was attributed to alcoholic gastritis, which improved with proton-pump inhibitor therapy. He exhibited symptoms of alcohol withdrawal, including anxiety and paresthesias, and was treated with IV diazepam. Despite medical advice, he chose to leave the hospital early. Psychiatry confirmed his decisional capacity, and he was discharged on a six-day oral diazepam taper, thiamine, and his usual medications. He demonstrated understanding of the risks and committed to outpatient follow-up.

radiology_notes.text:
HISTORY:  Alcoholic.  Evaluate pancreatitis.

TECHNIQUE:  CT the abdomen was performed with and without IV contrast. 
Multiplanar images were reformatted.

COMPARISON:  ___.

FINDINGS: The lung bases and imaged portion of the cardiac apex are
unremarkable.  Within the abdomen there is splenomegaly (15 cm, unchanged
given measurement technique differences since the prior study) as well as a
hepatomegaly and a mildly nodular contour of the liver.  Several large varices
along with a patent para-umbilical vein reflect underlying portal
hypertension. There is no peripancreatic fluid collections, stranding or
pseudocyst. No pancreatic calcifications are present to suggest CT evidence of
chronic pancreatitis. 

Bilateral adrenals and kidneys are normal.   Imaged portion the bowel appears
normal.  No abdominal free fluid is noted.  The gallbladder appears
unremarkable. The visualized aorta is of normal caliber.

No suspicious lytic or sclerotic lesions are identified. Endplate deformities
of T9 are stable as is the compression fracture of T7.

IMPRESSION:

1. No CT evidence of pancreatitis.   

2. Cirrhosis and portal hypertension with hepatomegaly, splenomegaly and
multiple large varices.

3.  Stable compression fracture or T7 and superior enplate compression
fracture of T9.
